strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations in existing generative model evaluation metrics, with clear examples of failure modes

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN, FFHQ) with systematic metric evaluation tests demonstrating superiority over baselines on robustness, sensitivity, and interpretability
Clear presentation with good pedagogical examples (e.g., Figure 2) and extensive supplementary materials supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates practical value with metrics achieving linear degradation with bad sample proportion and bounded [0,1] scores
Theoretical grounding through Lemma 1 providing principled calibration approach for Clipped Coverage
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty—clipping contributions to 1 and radii to median are straightforward stabilization techniques rather than fundamental methodological innovations

Weak theoretical contributions—Lemma 1 assumes identical distributions (rarely satisfied in practice) and the proof uses standard order statistics without deeper insights; Clipped Density lacks theoretical analysis

Interpretability claims are overclaimed—linear degradation calibration only holds when bad samples reliably fall outside all real balls, not under realistic distribution shifts or continuous degradation

Strong assumptions underlying calibration are not validated; Clipped Density normalization depends on real data quality via leave-one-out evaluation, potentially violating robustness claims when real data contains outliers

Limited real-world validation—experiments primarily use synthetic bad sample injection rather than natural distribution shifts, and Section F (chest X-rays) shows low scores without validating predictive value or correlation with downstream performance

Incomplete benchmark comparison—Tables 7-8 show failures on several Raisä et al. tests; dismissing these as 'harsh criteria' or 'incorrect criterion' (Section H) weakens claims rather than addressing them rigorously
All image results depend on DINOv2-ViT-L/14 embedding choice, yet authors acknowledge embedding comparison remains an open question; missing sensitivity analysis across embeddings
Arbitrary design choices lack principled justification—median radius clipping is intuitive but unjustified, k=5 appears arbitrary, and alternative clipping functions unexplored
Missing guidance on practical hyperparameter selection; hyperparameter sensitivity (Section K) shows metrics still vary with k but no dataset-specific tuning recommendations provided

strengths: Addresses important and timely problem in generative model evaluation identified by recent position papers
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple sanity checks on synthetic and real datasets
Clear motivation with effective illustrative examples (Figure 2)
Theoretical contribution via Lemma 1 for Clipped Coverage calibration
Extensive implementation details, reproducibility discussion, and appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core ideas are straightforward engineering modifications (clipping, median-based normalization) rather than conceptually novel approaches
Weak theoretical justification: choice of median for radius clipping is heuristic, normalization by real data lacks formal grounding, extension of Lemma 1 to mixed cases is assumed without proof

Overstated interpretability claims: assumption that bad samples affect metrics linearly and independently is unjustified; no validation that practitioners find absolute score interpretation meaningful
Embedding model dependency: evaluation relies on DINOv2 but sensitivity to embedding choice is not thoroughly investigated, undermining 'absolute interpretability' claim
Critical design choices appear post-hoc and arbitrary: median clipping, leave-one-out calibration, numerical function g for Coverage lack principled justification
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: no exploration of performance under structured failures, spatial clustering of bad samples, or different types of distribution shifts
Limited practical validation: no user studies, practitioner evaluation, or evidence that absolute scores guide model selection decisions differently than relative comparisons
Benchmark alignment issues: disagreements with Räisä et al. (2025) criteria suggest potential misalignment in evaluation philosophy

strengths: Addresses important, well-motivated problem (absolute interpretability in generative model evaluation) identified as critical gap by recent position paper
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple synthetic test scenarios, 12+ baseline comparisons, and 4 large-scale datasets; clear evidence of consistent improvements
Strong theoretical contribution: Lemma 1 provides rigorous analysis enabling principled calibration; clear mathematical formulation with good intuition for design choices
Metrics achieve desirable interpretability property (linear degradation with proportion of bad samples, normalization to [0,1]) that no existing metric provides
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (Figures 1-5), and thorough implementation details supporting reproducibility
Robust empirical results: Only proposed metrics consistently pass all test scenarios across Figures 4e and 5c
Good ablation studies (Section E) quantifying effects of individual components; sensitivity analysis provided (Section K)
weaknesses: Design choices lack sufficient theoretical justification: median-based radius clipping appears ad-hoc (why median vs. other quantiles?); leave-one-out normalization for ClippedDensity seems unprincipled and requires access to real data distribution

Theoretical analysis incomplete: Lemma 1 assumes identical distributions but behavior under distribution shift unexplored; calibration procedure (insertion index in sorted list) lacks stability/convergence analysis

Representation model dependence underexplored: metrics computed in DINOv2 embedding space but robustness to different embeddings, domains, or modalities not investigated; acknowledged as open question but deserves more attention

Interpretation of absolute scores potentially misleading: claiming score 0.4 means '40% good samples' oversimplifies; limited guidance on what scores mean across different dataset sizes or application domains; single medical imaging example insufficient

Benchmark evaluation shows remaining issues: ClippedCoverage still fails multiple tests in Räisä et al. benchmark; paper argues some failures should be successes, suggesting unresolved limitations in either metrics or benchmark

Real-world validation severely limited: vast majority of experiments on standard vision benchmarks; only one medical imaging example (Section F) with minimal discussion; no evaluation on non-image domains or actual deployment scenarios

Computational complexity underspecified: while wall-clock times reported, no Big-O complexity analysis; scalability to billions of samples in high dimensions unclear; ball-tree space requirements not discussed
Hyperparameter selection unjustified: k=5 used throughout but justification limited; Section K shows non-trivial sensitivity; guidance for choosing k on new datasets missing

strengths: Addresses real and important problem: existing fidelity/coverage metrics are vulnerable to outliers and out-of-distribution samples, with concrete motivating examples
Comprehensive experimental validation: extensive controlled experiments with known ground truth, evaluation on 4 major datasets with 50+ additional experiments in appendices
Strong empirical validation: demonstrates correlation with human judgments (r > 0.85), tests diverse model types and edge cases across multiple scenarios
Practical utility: provides interpretable absolute scores in [0,1] range without requiring reference models, valuable for practitioners
Theoretically grounded: Lemma 1 provides analytical justification; clear desiderata are stated and satisfied; calibration procedure is mathematically principled
Thorough robustness analysis: tests sensitivity to hyperparameters, distortions, truncation levels, rare modes, and various failure scenarios
Well-executed and clear presentation: good writing quality, clear figures, logical organization, and promises code release for reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: clipping outlier contributions and normalization are relatively straightforward techniques; applies clipping + normalization to existing Naeem et al. (2020) Density/Coverage framework; feels incremental compared to recent alternatives like Precision Cover/Recall Cover

Incomplete theoretical analysis: Lemma 1 only covers special case where real and synthetic distributions are identical; lacks analysis for general distribution pairs or infinite sample limits; missing finite-sample convergence rates or concentration bounds

Hyperparameter selection not well justified: choice of clipping thresholds (radius 1, mass 1) appears arbitrary; k parameter selection (Section L) lacks principled guidance despite shown sensitivity; no clear methodology for practitioners to choose these values

Calibration methodology concerns: normalization for ClippedCoverage requires numerically complex procedures (solving for specific index values); assumes mixture quality model that may not hold universally; less rigorous than ideal

Limited scope beyond image generation: vast majority of experiments focus on images; time series and music examples (Section P) are toy-level with minimal analysis; claims about generality to all generative models not fully supported

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and applicability: limited guidance on when NOT to use metrics; assumes nearest-neighbor structure meaningful in embedding space (not universal); no discussion of minimum sample size or dimensional requirements

Edge case interpretation issues: metrics can exceed 1 with certain models (Section K); interpretation as filtered real distribution is somewhat philosophical; potentially confusing for users despite explanation

Benchmark comparison somewhat defensive (Section H): discrepancies with Räisä et al. (2025) explained by implementation details raising reproducibility questions; arguments about criterion strictness lack objectivity

Reproducibility and implementation concerns: calibration procedure complexity could make reproduction difficult; numerical precision in solving index values matters; implementation details critical but not exhaustive

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear identification of limitations in existing metrics (Precision, Recall, Density, Coverage) regarding outlier robustness and score calibration

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, ImageNet, LSUN Bedroom, FFHQ) with systematic test scenarios demonstrating metric behavior under mode dropping, OOD samples, and synthetic corruptions
Rigorous experimental design with multiple test conditions (Figures 4-5, Sections 5-6) providing thorough validation of claimed properties
Mathematical rigor with formal metric definitions (Equations 5-10), theoretical analysis (Lemma 1), and calibration proofs
Practical utility with provided implementation, efficiency analysis (Section B.3), and computational complexity discussion
Honest acknowledgment of limitations, edge cases (Section K), and engagement with recent benchmarking work (Section H)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Core contribution is incremental engineering—applying standard robustification techniques (clipping outliers using k-NN radii, then linear calibration). The approach lacks conceptual novelty; clipping to median distance is intuitive but not deeply insightful

Circular evaluation design: Metrics are designed to satisfy specific synthetic test cases (Figures 4-5), then validated primarily on those same scenarios. Risk of overfitting to controlled test cases rather than capturing fundamental properties relevant to practitioners

Undemonstrated practical necessity: Paper fails to show that real generative models cause the problems demonstrated in synthetic scenarios, or that model rankings/selection decisions would meaningfully change using these metrics instead of existing ones (FID, IS)

Lack of principled design justification: Why is median-distance clipping optimal vs. alternatives? Why is the specific calibration function (Eq. 10) the right choice? Choices are empirically validated but lack theoretical foundation

Weak validation against human judgment: Section G only compares to human error rates for real/generated distinction; doesn't demonstrate these metrics predict human preferences for sample quality better than baselines. Human correlation shown but not compared to FID/IS

Lemma 1 relies on circular assumption: Proof assumes real and synthetic samples are identically distributed—precisely what these metrics cannot verify. This undermines the theoretical contribution's validity

Computational complexity under-analyzed: Claims efficiency but Equation 7 requires O(M) metric evaluations for normalization. Section M shows calibration requires 50 repetitions to achieve stable std < 0.002, suggesting brittleness

Problematic engagement with Raissi et al. (2025) benchmark: Rather than acknowledging potential metric limitations when benchmark tests fail (Section H), paper redefines success criteria and dismisses results as 'harsh criteria,' suggesting defensive reasoning
Limited hyperparameter analysis: Section L's k-sensitivity only tested on one dataset (DINOv2-FFHQ). Robustness of metrics across different k values and datasets under-explored
Narrow scope: Evaluation limited to image generation. Generalization to other modalities (text, audio, video) and generation paradigms (diffusion, flow, autoregressive) unclear
Missing practical examples: No concrete demonstrations that practitioners building generative models would reach different conclusions using these metrics vs. standard alternatives
